title: EcoVadis on Data Quality in Supply Chain Decarbonisation
content:
EcoVadis on Data Quality in Supply Chain Decarbonisation
Prioritise Us
on Google
EcoVadis and Kearney explore how poor data is a barrier to supply chain decarbonisation (Credit: EcoVadis)
Kearny’s Angela Hultberg & Ecovadis’ Dexter Galvin discuss barriers to long-term decarbonisation within global supply chain networks
Supply chain emissions present the greatest decarbonisation challenge facing global businesses today. For organisations with complex procurement networks spanning multiple tiers and geographies, Scope 3 emissions – those generated across the value chain through purchased goods and services, logistics and product use – typically comprise 70 to 90% of total carbon output, according to the Science Based Targets initiative.
Yet despite representing the bulk of most companies' environmental impact, these indirect emissions remain the most difficult to quantify and address. The gap between climate commitments and operational capability is widening, particularly as research suggests many organisations could be
significantly underestimating
their true supply chain footprint.
A collaborative study between EcoVadis and management consultancy Kearney has examined carbon performance across more than 56,000 assessed companies, revealing critical insights into how data reliability affects decarbonisation progress throughout global supply networks. The findings point to an uncomfortable truth: without accurate carbon intelligence from suppliers, procurement teams cannot identify emission hotspots, prioritise interventions or allocate capital effectively.
We cannot let the pursuit of perfect data become an excuse for delay, we need good data for good decisions, and we need those decisions turned into action and impact.
Angela Hultberg, Global Head of Sustainability at Kearney
The supply chain data deficit
EcoVadis's 2026 Carbon Action Report, developed alongside Kearney, draws on carbon-performance information from 56,061 companies evaluated through the Carbon Action Manager platform between July 2025 and June 2026. The research examines the relationship between data quality, carbon-management maturity and supplier engagement across industries including manufacturing, retail, transport, technology and professional services.
According to the report, companies could be underestimating upstream Scope 3 emissions by as much as 2.7 times when relying on low-reliability data. This measurement gap has direct implications for
procurement strategy,
supplier relationship management and supply chain resilience planning.
"We cannot let the pursuit of perfect data become an excuse for delay, we need good data for good decisions, and we need those decisions turned into action and impact," says Angela Hultberg, Global Head of Sustainability at Kearney.
The analysis reveals that while 40% of companies in the EcoVadis network report Scope 3 emissions, only 4% use primary supplier data. The average company's upstream Scope 3 emissions are 27 times greater than its Scope 1 and 2 emissions combined. Companies using low-reliability data report a median Scope 3 multiplier of 2.5 times, compared with 6.8 times for companies using high-reliability or verified data – suggesting widespread underreporting among organisations without robust supplier engagement.
Angela Hultberg, Global Sustainability Director at Kearney
Concentrated emissions across supplier networks
One finding holds particular significance for
procurement professionals
: supply chain emissions are concentrated among a relatively small group of highly connected suppliers. The top 10% of emitters account for 95% of reported Scope 1 and 2 emissions across the network, and those high-emitting suppliers are connected to an average of 72 buyers, compared with 35 for the remaining 90%.
This concentration creates an opportunity for targeted intervention. Rather than attempting simultaneous engagement across entire supplier bases, procurement teams can prioritise relationships with the businesses responsible for the greatest emissions and serving the largest number of customers. Improving the data reliability of one major supplier could strengthen Scope 3 calculations for dozens of buyers simultaneously.
"The encouraging part is that
supply chains
are interconnected," Angela continues. "When a company works with its suppliers to improve data and reduce emissions, the impact extends far beyond its own operations. That is how progress scales, and if there is one thing we need, it is scale at speed."
Yet only 7% of companies currently engage suppliers on carbon reduction. This represents both a challenge and an opportunity. The report shows that companies engaging suppliers are roughly six times more likely to deliver on science-based targets, while companies with high-reliability or verified Scope 1 and 2 data reduce operational emissions 50% faster than lower-reliability peers.
Dexter Galvin, SVP Climate & Climate Ambassador, Ecovadis speaking as part of the Global Decarbonisation Strategies panel at Sustainability LIVE London 2026
The partnership between EcoVadis, which provides
sustainability intelligence
and supplier-assessment tools, and Kearney, which contributes expertise in procurement operations and supply chain transformation, positions Scope 3 emissions within broader business considerations including cost management and resilience.
The report argues that better carbon data should be treated as an operational tool rather than a compliance output. Companies that combine credible measurement with focused supplier engagement could be better positioned to reduce emissions, manage costs and build resilient value chains against climate-related disruption.
"Climate change continues to batter supply chains, deepening disruption just as new geopolitical realities have made building resilience even harder," says Dexter Galvin, Senior Vice President (SVP) and Climate Ambassador at EcoVadis. "With the systemic shocks of the past year still taking hold and a super El Niño strengthening – already forecast to cost the global economy nearly US$1tn in 2027 – many companies remain dangerously unprepared for what lies ahead."
Key statistics
Scope 3 emissions typically represent 70 to 90% of a company’s total emissions
40% of companies in the EcoVadis network report Scope 3 emissions, but only 4% use primary supplier data
Companies using low-reliability data report a median Scope 3 multiplier of 2.5x, compared with 6.8x for companies using high-reliability or verified data
Only 7% of companies currently engage suppliers on carbon
Companies engaging suppliers are roughly 6x more likely to deliver on science-based targets
Companies with high-reliability or verified Scope 1 and 2 data reduce operational emissions 50% faster than lower-reliability peers
Companies acting across governance, targets, reporting, Scope 1 and 2 and Scope 3 reduce operational emissions nearly twice as fast as those acting across three or fewer areas
Leading companies combine contractual requirements with tailored support, incentives and collaboration. Examples in the report include Atos' high-touch engagement with priority suppliers, Becton Dickinson (BD)'s use of manufacturing experts to identify practical reductions and Accor's supplier recognition programme. Companies acting across governance, targets, reporting, Scope 1 and 2 and Scope 3 reduce operational emissions nearly twice as fast as those acting across three or fewer areas.
The next phase of supply chain decarbonisation will move beyond company-level emissions towards product carbon footprints, enabling buyers to compare the embedded carbon of specific materials, components and products. For sectors such as automotive, manufacturing, retail and construction, product-level data could help shift procurement from broad emissions estimates to targeted interventions at the source. However, this requires investment in supplier capabilities, common methodologies and data-sharing across
industry networks
"The report shows that a surprisingly large number of companies are still not actively working on reducing scope 3 emissions," Angela adds. "The silver lining of that is that we can potentially see a lot of reduction really fast, because the solutions and best practices are out there to learn from, you just need to get going."
Companies featured in the report
EcoVadis
EcoVadis is the report’s publisher and the organisation behind the Carbon Action Manager platform. It provides sustainability ratings, carbon-management tools, supplier-risk assessments, training and worker-voice solutions to businesses worldwide.
Kearney is a global management consultancy and co-contributor to the report. Its sustainability specialists contributed analysis and commentary on supply-chain resilience, carbon data and decarbonisation. Kearney works with companies and governments in more than 40 countries, helping organisations address strategic, operational and sustainability challenges. It serves many large multinational businesses and much of the Fortune Global 500.
Hitachi Rail
Hitachi Rail is presented in the report as an example of a company embedding supplier decarbonisation into procurement and operational decision-making. Its Head of Supplier Sustainability sits within the procurement function, helping ensure that climate objectives influence buying decisions. Hitachi Rail tailors supplier engagement according to maturity: advanced suppliers may discuss science-based targets and product-level carbon data, while less mature suppliers begin with basic measurement and reporting. The company has also started discussing product carbon footprints with key suppliers.
Accor is a global hospitality group featured in the report as an example of collaborative supplier decarbonisation. Its approach is organised around three pillars: Measure, Reduce and Promote. Accor first assesses supplier maturity, then seeks corporate emissions data before moving towards product-level information and carbon footprints. The company also uses supplier recognition, including carbon medals, to encourage progress through commercial visibility and competition. Accor supports sector collaboration through the Hospitality Alliance for Responsible Procurement, which aligns buyers around a shared supplier framework.
Atos is identified in the report as a company using cross-functional governance and targeted supplier engagement to advance Scope 3 action. Its procurement and sustainability teams meet every two weeks to review priorities and individual supplier emissions. Atos also sets detailed regional targets covering which suppliers require assessment, support or onboarding. The company prioritises approximately 200 suppliers globally for high-touch engagement, offering guidance tailored to their maturity. It has adjusted its contracting approach after finding that rigid year-on-year reduction requirements were not always practical.
BD, formerly known as Becton, Dickinson and Company, is cited in the report for integrating supplier sustainability closely with procurement. Its supplier sustainability team is embedded within procurement, with senior procurement involvement when engagement stalls. BD makes science-based targets a condition of preferred-supplier status and uses a maturity ladder to create staged improvement pathways. Its manufacturing experts visit supplier sites to identify low-cost or no-cost emissions reductions. BD also maps carbon intensity to specific purchased materials, supporting lower-carbon sourcing decisions.
Unilever
Unilever is an EcoVadis customer and, as a major consumer-goods company, it represents the type of organisation for which Scope 3 emissions, supplier data and purchasing decisions are especially important. Consumer-goods businesses often have extensive upstream footprints spanning agricultural commodities, packaging, chemicals, manufacturing and distribution. The report’s findings suggest that companies such as Unilever can benefit from reliable primary supplier data, targeted engagement with high-impact suppliers and collaboration across shared supply chains.
Bridgestone
Bridgestone appears in the report as one of the companies using EcoVadis services. Tyre manufacturing involves energy-intensive production and complex supply chains covering natural and synthetic rubber, chemicals, steel, logistics and other materials. Those characteristics make supplier carbon measurement and product-level emissions data particularly important to effective Scope 3 management.
BASF is named among EcoVadis’s customers. The chemical sector is directly relevant to the report's central argument because chemicals and industrial materials are often energy-intensive and embedded throughout downstream value chains. Reliable emissions data from chemical suppliers can influence procurement, product design and customer Scope 3 calculations. BASF’s inclusion illustrates how the report’s data and supplier-engagement themes apply to large industrial businesses with complex, interconnected supply networks.

title: XPeng shops its self-driving tech to automakers — Tesla found no takers
content:
XPeng is trying to turn its self-driving and smart-cockpit systems into a licensing business, courting automakers, suppliers, and software firms well beyond its existing Volkswagen deal, according to a Reuters report.
It’s the exact playbook Tesla has been pitching for years with “Full Self-Driving.” The difference is that XPeng is finding interest.
The Chinese EV maker set up a “strategic commercialisation team” about six months ago to chase these deals, Reuters reported. On offer: its electrical and electronic vehicle architecture, its smart cockpit, its in-house Turing AI chips, ADAS and autonomous-driving software, and even its robotaxi and humanoid-robot work. No new customers have been named, but XPeng says interested parties have already made contact, and that they could include foreign software developers and auto suppliers as well as carmakers.
The Volkswagen blueprint
The template for all of this is Volkswagen. VW put roughly $700 million into XPeng in 2023 for a 4.99% stake, then leaned on the startup’s software and electronics for its own China-market EVs. The jointly developed ID.UNYX 08 electric SUV entered mass production in March 2026 running XPeng’s tech.
That deal is already showing up on XPeng’s books. Service revenue jumped 93.9% year-over-year to about $400 million in the second quarter of 2026. That’s the high-margin, non-hardware income this whole licensing push is built to scale, and it’s a big reason the stock ticked up around 3% on the report. XPEV is still down about 47% year-to-date.
Tesla has wanted this for years
Selling your self-driving stack to other automakers is precisely what Elon Musk has been trying to do with FSD since 2021, and he keeps coming up empty.
Musk floated “preliminary discussions” with other carmakers in 2021, said Tesla was “happy to license” its tech after a 2023 charging deal with Ford, and claimed in April 2024 that Tesla was “in talks with one major automaker” about FSD. None of it produced a signed licensing deal.
Then, last November, Musk admitted the automakers simply don’t want it. “I’ve tried to warn them and even offered to license Tesla FSD, but they don’t want it! Crazy…” he wrote on X. Ford CEO Jim Farley had already said the quiet part out loud, telling the public that “Waymo is better.” Part of the standoff is liability: legacy automakers reportedly wanted Tesla to eat the risk when a licensed system crashes, and Musk called those terms unworkable.
A vision-first stack that kept its safety net
XPeng’s approach to self-driving actually rhymes with Tesla’s. When we interviewed XPeng’s head of AI earlier this year, Dr. Xianming Liu described the same core philosophy: scale up the data, train end-to-end neural networks, and let the car drive on cameras.
But XPeng didn’t gut the sensor suite to get there. Where Tesla deleted radar and ultrasonics in pursuit of pure vision, XPeng keeps them as a separate, redundant safety layer that runs independently of the main driving AI. “We do utilize these other sensors, but they are utilized for the active safety system, which requires an orthogonal system to be totally redundant with the main driving system,” Liu told us. Those sensors power automatic emergency braking and steering as a backstop, even though cameras do the actual driving. It’s the same vision-led bet Tesla made, with a hardware safety net Tesla threw out.
For a potential licensing customer nervous about handing driving decisions to a neural network, that redundancy is an easier sell than “cameras only, trust us.” We drove XPeng’s latest system earlier this year, and it made clear Tesla no longer has the “Full Self-Driving” space to itself.
Electrek’s Take
Top comment by Beario
We will see how all of this plays out, but I keep thinking at some point Tesla is going to have to put some sort of sensor system back into their cars and they will only say that the are following government regulations. The cybercab is also being scrutinized for lack of a backup or sensor system so it may not actually be acceptable in some areas. It certainly will be interesting to see how it plays out here with the deployment, but Waymo certainly has no issues deploying cars everywhere.
This is a neat little role reversal. A Chinese EV startup is now the self-driving and electronics supplier to Volkswagen, and it’s shopping that same package to whoever else is behind on software. Tesla has spent half a decade insisting it would be the one to license FSD to the industry, and it hasn’t landed a single deal.
The reason XPeng is getting traction and Tesla isn’t comes down to a few unglamorous things. XPeng actually ships to a paying reference customer, with VW mass-producing cars on its stack right now. It kept a redundant safety system, which makes the tech easier to underwrite. And it’s happy to act as a supplier rather than demanding to be the platform everyone bows to. Tesla wants the platform economics without taking on the crash liability, and it still can’t point to an unsupervised product it has delivered to the people who already paid for it –aka all of us FSD owners.
The obvious caveat is geopolitics. A US or European automaker licensing Chinese autonomous-driving software and Chinese AI chips is a hard sell in the current climate of data-security reviews and tariffs. So the near-term buyers are probably other Chinese brands, emerging-market automakers, and suppliers rather than Detroit or Wolfsburg’s rivals. Still, the direction of travel is the thing to watch.

title: Volkswagen's EV van drove through 92 countries to set a new Guinness World Record
content:
Volkswagen
VW ID BUZZ
Volkswagen ID Buzz
Peter Johnson
| Sep 18 2026 - 7:26 am PT
Volkswagen ID. Buzz
set a new Guinness World Record for “the most countries visited in a continuous journey” by an EV, covering nearly 100,000 km across 92 countries.
VW ID. Buzz receives Guinness World Record for an EV
After 445 days of travel, crossing 92 countries and covering 99,767 km, or about 62,000 miles, Volkswagen’s electric van earned its place in the Guinness World Records.
Rainer Zietlow drove the ID. Buzz Long Wheelbase (LWB) “around the world,” across six continents, through major cities, deserts and mountains.
Starting in Hanover, Germany, Volkswagen took the electric van to every part of the globe, including through the US, Africa, South America, Europe, the Middle East, Southeast Asia, Australia, and China.
It took more than 300 charging cycles and 16 container ships, but Volkswagen’s electric van completed the entire trip without a single technical breakdown.
Guinness World Records representative, Lena Kuhlmann, presented the certificate for the “Most countries visited in a continuous journey by a battery powered electric vehicle” at IAA Transportation 2026.
Rainer Zietlow receives the certificate from Guinness World Records representative Lena Kuhlmann (Source: Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles)
“I had no technical problems,” Zietlow said in an interview at the event. Following the trip, Hanover-based
TÜV Nord
certified the ID. Buzz’s high-voltage battery retained 95.75% state of health.
Zietlow said the trip was his “biggest project in 20 years, at one year and four months,” and the longest he had ever undertaken.
“I am particularly proud that we came through this high mileage without any technical problems, and that through genuinely difficult regions,” the driver said during the interview.
Volkswagen ID. Buzz in Thailand as it earns Guinness World Record for “Most countries visited in a continuous journey by a battery powered electric vehicle” Source: Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles)
Zietlow explained that “On a trip like this, the difference between a combustion engine and an electric vehicle is noticeable. In many parts of the world, diesel fuel can contain high sulphur levels or water contamination, several oil changes are required and there is also the risk of the engine overheating,” adding that “all of that is eliminated with an electric vehicle.”
Volkswagen ID. Buzz in the US as it earns Guinness World Record for “Most countries visited in a continuous journey by a battery powered electric vehicle” Source: Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles)
Even when you factor in charging, “you are better off with an electric car,” he said. As battery and other EV components advance, travel will be easier and more efficient than ever.
“The gap to the combustion engine is getting smaller,” Zietlow told reporters, adding that “If the solid-state battery arrives at some point, along with very fast hyper-charging, then a great deal more will be possible.”
Volkswagen ID. Buzz in the US as it earns Guinness World Record for “Most countries visited in a continuous journey by a battery powered electric vehicle” Source: Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles)
Soon, “in the not-too-distant future,” he added, “the combustion engine will be to us what the horse-drawn carriage once was.”
The Guinness World Record was achieved in a series production ID. Buzz. Volkswagen used an ID. Buzz Pro Long Wheelbase (LWB) model.
VW’s electric van uses an 86 kWh battery that provides a WLTP range of up to 498 km. With DC fast-charging up to 200 kW, the ID. Buzz Pro LWB’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in under 30 minutes.

title: 144 Tesla Megapacks power Australia’s first 8-hour grid battery
content:
Fred Lambert
| Sep 18 2026 - 7:12 am PT
Australia just switched on its longest-duration grid battery, and it runs on 144 Tesla Megapacks.
RWE’s Limondale battery in New South Wales can discharge for a full eight hours — four times longer than the two-hour batteries that dominate the Australian grid. It’s the first project of its kind in the country.
The battery sits at 50 MW / 400 MWh, near Balranald in the state’s south-west, right next to RWE’s existing Limondale solar farm. It’s now registered and operating on the National Electricity Market after getting its final operational sign-off from grid operator AEMO earlier this year.
Charging twice as fast as it discharges
Limondale is built to charge at roughly 100 MW but discharge at only 50 MW. Most grid batteries charge and discharge at the same rate. This one doesn’t.
That asymmetry is the whole point. The battery can fill up in about four hours — soaking up the midday solar glut when NSW is drowning in cheap renewable power — then stretch that energy back out over eight hours to cover the evening peak and into the night. Charge fast, discharge slow.
It’s a neat answer to the “duck curve” problem that every solar-heavy grid runs into: too much power at noon, not enough at 7 PM. Pairing the battery directly with a solar farm makes the arbitrage even cleaner.
Why 8-hour storage is the new frontier
Australia has plenty of big batteries. What it hasn’t had is long ones.
The first wave of grid storage, including Tesla’s landmark Hornsdale project, was built for fast response and one-to-two hours of duration, great for grid stability, useless for shifting bulk solar into the evening. Four-hour batteries are now becoming the norm. Eight hours is the next step up, and Limondale is the proof of concept.
RWE didn’t build it on spec. Limondale was the only winning bid in NSW’s first long-duration storage tender under the state’s Electricity Infrastructure Roadmap, backed by a Long-Term Energy Service Agreement, essentially a government revenue floor that makes financing a long battery bankable. Two more LTESA-backed 8-hour batteries are moving through the NSW pipeline behind it.
“RWE’s investment decision and signing of supplier contracts for the Limondale BESS project is an exciting step forward,” RWE Renewables Europe & Australia CEO Katja Wünschel said when the project was greenlit. Tesla supplied the Megapacks; Beon Energy Solutions handled the balance of plant.
For Tesla, it’s another flagship win in a market it helped create. The company has been stacking up grid deals worldwide, from a
500 MWh Megapack battery that just went live in Texas
1 GWh project in the UK
, and its
Megapack
energy business is now one of its fastest-growing segments.
Electrek’s Take
Two-hour batteries proved storage could stabilize a grid. Eight-hour batteries are what actually let you retire coal, because they can carry solar generation through the entire evening ramp instead of tapping out at dinnertime. That’s the transition Australia is trying to pull off, and it’s why the asymmetric charge/discharge design matters more than it looks. Building a battery that inhales cheap midday solar and exhales it slowly all night is exactly the shape of storage a renewables-heavy grid needs.
Now, we just need a lot more of them.
Home batteries are quietly changing the economics of residential energy the same way grid batteries are reshaping the wholesale market, and pairing one with rooftop solar is the best way to squeeze the most value out of both. This week, the US House of Representatives voted overwhelmingly in a bipartisan vote to renew funding for the Diesel Emissions Reduction Act (DERA), passing the measure 343-79 and extending federal funding for cleaner medium- and heavy-duty vehicles through 2029.
Proving once again that everyone can get behind reducing air pollution, saving money on fuel, and AM radio, the House passed 14 bills this week, including House Resolution 2140 that amends section 797(a) of the Energy Policy Act of 2005 to extend the authorization of the Diesel Emissions Reduction Act grant program to 2029. Introduced by Reps. Doris Matsui (D-CA), Ken Calvert (R-CA), Chellie Pingree (D-ME), and Nick Langworthy (R-NY), the bipartisan legislation authorized $100 million in annual for the long-running program through fiscal year 2029.
“Through the diligent work of the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, we are preserving the public health and safety of our communities, lowering electricity prices for hardworking families, and promoting a vibrant tourism industry that uplifts communities across the country,” said Congressman Brett Guthrie (KY-02), Chairman of the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, in a statement.

. “By passing this bipartisan legislation, the House has taken an important step toward ensuring carriers can continue modernizing their fleets, which will deliver fuel savings and further emissions reductions.”

title: Regulatory uncertainty threatens to slow German PV deployment in 2027 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Germany’s PV sector remains buoyant in 2026, but regulatory uncertainty and tighter financing conditions are raising fears of a downturn. Without transitional measures, proposed limits on grid feed-in could trigger widespread insolvencies and a sharp market contraction in 2027.
Martin Schachinger, pvXchange
18 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Ask most PV installers in Germany, and they will say they are broadly satisfied with 2026. Some even describe it as their best year in a long time. At the same time, reports of insolvencies among major solar companies are mounting. Project developer Enerparc and manufacturer RCT Power are only the most prominent German examples.
Such news is causing concern, particularly among industry veterans who remember the period from 2012 to 2014. After three consecutive strong years, drastic subsidy cuts championed by then-Federal Environment Minister Peter Altmaier (CDU) pushed more than half of Germany’s solar companies into financial distress and, sooner or later, out of the market. The resulting collapse in installations became known as the “Altmaier effect.” Are we now facing a “Reiche effect,” named after Katherina Reiche, Germany’s federal minister for economic affairs and energy?
There are currently no significant changes in module prices. PV component costs are declining moderately, although price increases have already been announced in the battery segment. Whether these increases can be implemented – and how long they might last – remains to be seen. The high cost of fossil fuel-based energy and supply chain disruption along some shipping routes to Europe must also be taken into account. Ultimately, however, market prices are determined by supply and demand.
Demand in Germany remains high. Established installation companies have full order books through the end of the year and little capacity to take on new projects. The question is how long this favorable situation can last, particularly under the shadow of the so-called Reiche effect.
The relevant bills have yet to pass the Bundestag and Bundesrat, which are Germany’s lower and upper houses of parliament, respectively. However, there are concerns that provisions considered harmful to the PV sector will survive the legislative process and become law. Some German PV companies are invoking worst-case scenarios to attract customers, which may partly explain the current strength of demand. Many customers want to complete their projects this year to secure the existing conditions under the Renewable Energy Sources Act (EEG), fearing that commissioning at a later date could make their systems economically unviable.
That outcome is not inevitable and will depend on the business model, but it appears to reflect prevailing market sentiment. The rush to bring projects forward may already be distorting the market to an unhealthy degree.
Large project developers and PV suppliers are also feeling the effects. The temporary market upswing is creating strong demand for financing, but uncertainty – whether tolerated or politically induced – means that this demand cannot be met, or can be met only inadequately. Banks are becoming increasingly cautious about new financing requests and are tightening the terms of existing loans.
Removing the security that the EEG has historically provided as a backstop will inevitably create problems unless carefully designed transitional measures are introduced. This cannot be emphasized strongly enough. Unfortunately, such measures are largely absent from the legislation currently under consideration.
If the proposals – particularly the 50% cap on grid feed-in – remain unchanged in the coming weeks, the insolvencies already announced may mark only the beginning of a wave of closures reminiscent of the Altmaier era. In that scenario, even falling component prices would provide little relief.
If the feared market downturn materializes in 2027, only companies flexible enough to adopt alternative business models are likely to survive. Minister Reiche and the CDU-led government could then claim the dubious distinction of having driven an entire sector into crisis for a second time. In doing so, they would also have curtailed the inconvenient decentralization that, in their view, merely creates additional work and reduces profits for the traditional energy industry.

title: The Hydrogen Stream: Singapore researchers present artificial leaf for H2 production from contaminated seawater - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In other news, Power to Hydrogen started green hydrogen production in Antwerp, while Dongfeng unveiled three hydrogen-powered commercial vehicles in Hannover. Moreover, Denmark opened the EU’s first full-scale CO₂ storage site, and H2 Mobility began trial operations at a hydrogen refueling station at Hannover Airport.
Sergio Matalucci
18 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Hydrogen
Utility-scale
The artificial leaf uses solar energy to produce hydrogen from contaminated seawater via electrolysis.
Nanyang Technological University
has unveiled what it calls an artificial leaf – a perovskite device that uses solar energy to produce hydrogen from contaminated seawater via electrolysis. The process simultaneously degrades hydrazine, a highly toxic contaminant found in industrial wastewater. “They designed the anode with a catalyst that breaks down hydrazine into hydrogen and nitrogen. At the same time, the production of corrosive and toxic chlorine compounds from seawater is suppressed,” said the research team, led by Lydia Wong. The researchers fabricated the cathode from lead halide-based perovskites that capture light and convert it into electricity. “The photocurrent density – the amount of current generated per illuminated area of the device – was one of the highest reported for lead-based perovskite cathodes. The device maintained stable performance for more than 72 hours under illumination equivalent to the intensity of sunlight reaching the Earth’s surface on a clear day, generating hydrogen at a rate comparable to similar solar-powered devices,” they said. The researchers presented their findings in “
Self-powered artificial leaf using perovskite photocathode for solar hydrogen production and hydrazine degradation
,” published in
nature communications
Power to Hydrogen
(P2H2) has started commercial green hydrogen production in the NextGen District at the Port of Antwerp-Bruges. The 500 kW system, comprising two 250 kW stacks and delivered to the site in August, is reportedly the first commercial deployment of 250 kW anion exchange membrane (AEM) stacks. The US electrolyzer developer said the facility is more than 10 times larger than the stacks used in conventional AEM systems. “Now operational, the system will initially produce up to 70 tonnes of green hydrogen per year for regional gas supplier Holthausen and other customers in the area. The hydrogen will be used mainly for mobility customers, with other industrial use cases as an additional potential offtake,” the Ohio-based company said.
Dongfeng Motor Group
has presented three hydrogen-powered vehicles at a trade fair in Hannover, Germany: a workhorse for long-haul logistics, a dual electric-hydrogen truck, and an intercity truck for cold-chain deliveries. The vehicles are based on a platform featuring a 400 kW hydrogen fuel cell stack with efficiency of more than 58%. The system reportedly achieves hydrogen consumption as low as 7 kg per 100 km, while the vehicles have a curb weight starting at 8.8 tonnes.
The European Union’s first full-scale CO₂ storage site
has officially opened in Denmark. The country’s king inaugurated the Greensand CO₂ storage facility, which is led by Ineos Energy in partnership with Harbour Energy and the Danish North Sea Fund (Nordsøfonden). “Greensand expects to store up to 400,000 tonnes of CO₂ annually in this first commercial phase, scaling toward a potential of up to 4 million to 8 million tonnes annually at full capacity,” said Ineos.
H2 Mobility
has started trial operations at its new hydrogen refueling station at Hannover-Langenhagen Airport in Germany. Commercial vehicles and passenger cars can now refuel at the site. “Schreck + Batz Logistik, a logistics company based in Langenhagen, took delivery of a hydrogen truck for testing purposes,” said H2 Mobility, which develops, builds, and operates hydrogen refueling infrastructure for all vehicle classes.

title: French agrivoltaic trials cut water loss, lift maize yields by 19.6% - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
TSE’s agrivoltaic trials in France recorded barley yields of up to 96% of those in a control plot and reduced seasonal evapotranspiration by 20%. At a separate site, maize yield beneath the canopy was 19.6% higher during exceptionally hot and dry conditions.
Gwénaëlle Deboutte
18 Sep 2026
Applications & Installations
Utility-scale
French renewable energy producer TSE has reported results from agronomic monitoring at its agrivoltaic sites, including barley yields of up to 96% of those recorded in a control plot, a 20% reduction in seasonal evapotranspiration, and a 19.6% increase in maize yield under exceptionally hot and dry conditions.
TSE deployed an agrivoltaic canopy at a site in Chadeleuf, in the Puy-de-Dôme department of central France. The site was planted with winter forage barley, which was harvested in late June. It is equipped with 18 radiation sensors, 14 weather stations, and 14 probes that measure soil temperature and moisture.
Agronomic research company Antédis harvested the crop with an experimental combine harvester. The Puy-de-Dôme Chamber of Agriculture and the Limagne Centre for Technical Agricultural Studies (CETA) conducted the monitoring and validated the results.
Evapotranspiration falls by 20%
Initial comparisons with a control plot without solar panels showed that barley yields beneath the agrivoltaic canopy reached between 90% and 96% of those recorded in the control area.
“In all scenarios, the requirements of the decree of April 8, 2024, on the development of agrivoltaics – specifically, a yield loss of less than 10% – were met,” TSE said.
The company said its PV panel control system also reduced heat stress beneath the canopy. Grain specific weight, an indicator of quality, was 3% higher than in the control plot.
Evapotranspiration declined by 20% over the growing season, improving water management.
Canopy moderates temperature extremes
According to the agronomists, the canopy’s protective effect was most pronounced during periods of extreme heat. At the hottest time of day, the air temperature at crop level was 4.1 C lower beneath the panels. Evapotranspiration during these periods fell by 2.15 mm per day.
On the coldest nights, temperatures beneath the canopy were up to 3 C higher. Measurements taken in 2025 and 2026 at TSE’s agrivoltaic site in Brouchy showed that the structure reduced the average daily temperature range by about 1.5 C. Similar effects were observed beneath the Chadeleuf canopy in 2026.
Maize yield rises 19.6% at Amance
TSE also published results from its agrivoltaic canopy in Amance, in the Haute-Saône department of eastern France. Silage maize was planted at the site on April 25, 2026.
The crop faced severe weather stress during a spring and summer marked by exceptional drought and heat. A rainless April coincided with maize emergence, followed by hot, dry conditions during the final stages of stem elongation and flowering, when maize is particularly vulnerable. Temperatures in the open-field control plot exceeded 35 C.
“In this context, the canopy provided the expected protective effect,” TSE said.
Ear sterility was most prevalent in the control plot, although similar symptoms were also observed beneath the canopy. Maize plants beneath the canopy reached an average height of 200 cm, compared with 160 cm in the control plot.
Dry-matter yield was ultimately 19.6% higher beneath the canopy than in the control plot.
Although the maize grown beneath the panels was also affected by the exceptional heat, TSE said the agrivoltaic system helped mitigate the impact and secure a forage harvest. The company is processing the recently received crop-quality analysis.

title: Johnson Controls unveils industrial heat pump with 122 C output - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The Sabroe HitemHP uses butane or isobutane as its refrigerant and delivers between 100 kW and 1 MW of heating capacity. Johnson Controls says the single-stage system can operate at loads as low as 18% of its rated capacity.
Emiliano Bellini
18 Sep 2026
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
Heat pumps
The HitemHP heat pump
S-based industrial conglomerate
Johnson Controls
has launched an industrial heat pump capable of supplying hot water at temperatures of up to 122 C.
The company said its new Sabroe HitemHP system is intended to replace fossil-fuel and electric boilers in applications such as food and beverage processing, pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, chemicals and advanced manufacturing. It can also support pasteurization, sterilization and indirect steam production.
The heat pump is available in 10 configurations with nominal heating capacities ranging from approximately 100 kW to 1 MW. It uses a single-stage Sabroe SMC reciprocating compressor and a direct-expansion evaporator.
The system operates with natural hydrocarbon refrigerants R600, or n-butane, and R600a, or isobutane. Johnson Controls said the refrigerant circuit operates at pressures below 28 barg.
At a reference condition comprising a 50 C to 45 C evaporator-water circuit and a 100 C to 120 C condenser-water circuit, the manufacturer’s technical data show heating capacities of 125 kW to 511 kW. Shaft power consumption ranges from 45 kW to 173 kW, resulting in heating coefficients of performance (COP) of 2.8 to 3.0.
At a lower-temperature, with condenser water heated from 65 C to 103 C and the same evaporator conditions, the range delivers 240 kW to 964 kW. The corresponding heating COP is between 4.1 and 4.4.
Johnson Controls said the heat pump can reduce its output to 18% of rated capacity. It claims that part-load operation can raise COP by as much as 20% compared with full-load performance.
“Until now, electrifying high-temperature heat has been one of the hardest problems to solve,” said Steve Bell, vice president and general manager for industrial refrigeration at Johnson Controls.
The company said that, in one customer application combining the heat pump with waste heat from a refrigeration plant, the system achieved up to three times the energy efficiency of an electric boiler. It also estimated reductions of more than 91% in energy costs and up to 82% in on-site carbon dioxide emissions. The results were based on site-specific energy prices, water volumes and water-quality assumptions, according to the manufacturer.
The packaged units measure approximately 5.75 meters to 6.5 meters long, 1.25 meters wide and 2.25 meters high. Depending on the configuration, dry weight ranges from about 5.36 tonnes to 6.7 tonnes, while refrigerant charges range from 10 kg to 80 kg. Reported sound-pressure levels are between 85.1 dB(A) and 90.2 dB(A), measured at a distance of 1 meter.
The heat pumps are factory assembled and performance tested. Available options include variable-speed drives, separately mounted control panels and customer-witnessed factory acceptance testing.
Johnson Controls manufactures the HitemHP range at its facility in Holme, Denmark.

title: Google, esVolta pilot uses battery storage to ‘time-shift’ renewable energy credits - pv magazine Global
content: From ESS News oogle, battery storage developer esVolta, and clean-energy platforms Quintrace and LevelTen Energy have completed a three-month pilot testing a new commercial structure for storing surplus solar power. The project released stored power, along with hourly-verified renewable energy credits, during hours when Google’s electricity demand outpaced its renewable supply. Google sponsored the pilot to test whether battery storage can be used to “time-shift” renewable electricity and its associated environmental attributes. The project shifted a combined 9.2 GWh of solar-charged electricity through two of esVolta’s US battery energy storage systems: the 240 MW/480 MWh Anole project and the 100 MW/200 MWh Burksol project, together totaling 340 MW and 680 MWh of capacity. EsVolta has developed, owned and operated utility-scale battery projects across North America since 2017. Google identified specific daily windows when its electricity consumption was expected to exceed its available renewable supply. EsVolta charged its batteries with surplus solar generation during other hours and discharged that stored electricity, along with associated renewable energy credits, into those identified gap periods. Google did not toll the batteries or take on merchant or dispatch risk under the arrangement. EsVolta retained full operational control of the assets, including the ability to respond to price signals or grid emergencies outside the agreed windows. The renewable attributes involved in the pilot were tracked using “granular certificates,” a form of energy attribute certificate that carries an hourly timestamp rather than the monthly or annual aggregation used by conventional renewable energy certificates. Granular certificates are issued according to a standard developed by EnergyTag, a nonprofit organization. Quintrace verified each hour of battery charging and discharging against that standard, applying loss calculations to determine how much certified renewable electricity was actually delivered after storage. LevelTen managed the registry accounts underpinning the transactions to prevent the same renewable attributes from being counted more than once. The companies described the arrangement as the first publicly detailed commercial structure in which a corporate buyer contracts specifically to time-shift environmental attributes it already owns through battery storage, rather than purchasing new generation capacity or directly tolling a storage asset. The pilot is part of Google’s broader effort to match its electricity consumption with carbon-free energy on an hourly basis, rather than only on an annual net basis, as it works toward a stated goal of powering its data centers with 24/7 carbon-free energy by 2030. The tech group has reported matching 100% of its annual electricity consumption with renewable energy, but only around 65% of its consumption on an hourly basis, highlighting a gap it has said it is seeking to close through its 24/7 carbon-free energy strategy. Corporate carbon-accounting standards bodies have been evaluating whether and how to incorporate more granular electricity-matching concepts into their frameworks, but neither of the two major relevant standards has settled on a mandatory hourly-matching requirement. SBTi’s Corporate Net-Zero Standard, Version 2.0 , published in June, requires large electricity users – those consuming at least 10 GWh of electricity annually – to calculate and report their hourly renewable-matching rate. That reporting requirement becomes mandatory for larger companies when the standard opens for validation in February 2027. Actually achieving a high hourly-matching rate remains a separate, optional basis for recognition under the standard, rather than a requirement for target validation itself. The GHG Protocol , which sets the accounting rules most companies use for Scope 2 emissions reporting, has been evaluating similar changes but has not adopted a mandatory hourly-matching requirement. A public consultation on proposed revisions ran from October 2025 to January 2026 and drew more than 1,000 responses. Only about 22% of respondents, and roughly 12% of companies that responded, supported making hourly matching mandatory. Uncertainty over the pending revision has already been linked to a slowdown in corporate clean-power procurement, with corporate PPA volumes down 10% in 2025 as buyers waited for clarity on the rules. The GHG Protocol’s standards board has since directed its technical working group to develop multiple possible reporting approaches rather than a single mandatory rule, and a revised standard is not expected to be finalized until the end of 2028. The esVolta pilot follows several earlier steps in Google’s push toward granular carbon accounting. In 2023, the company ran a similar real-world test of hourly timestamped certificates with Danish utility Energinet and renewable energy supplier Better Energy, matching production and consumption data on an hourly basis for the first time. More recently, researchers have found that early corporate commitments to 24/7 carbon-free energy purchasing, even partial ones, could help lower costs for long-duration energy storage technologies by providing early revenue and real-world operating data – a dynamic the esVolta pilot’s storage-based time-shifting model appears designed to help capture. title: Inclusion by design: The leadership behaviours PV innovation needs - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Women in Solar+ Europe reflects this week on the leadership behaviours needed to strengthen innovation, psychological safety and collaboration across PV research and industry, following its workshop at EU PVSEC 2026 this week, co-organised with WIP Renewables. The discussion connected inclusion with how expertise shapes decisions. Its conclusions offer practical direction for PV teams and cross-sector partnerships.
Women in Solar+ Europe
18 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Innovation results from people combining expertise, questioning assumptions and learning across professional and organisational boundaries. It cannot reach its potential when seniority determines whose knowledge carries weight, concerns remain unspoken, or teams fail to develop collective intelligence.
This premise shaped “Diversity in PV: Embedding Inclusion by Design – The Leadership Behaviours Driving Innovation, High-Performing Research & Industry Teams,” delivered by Women in Solar+ Europe (WiSEu) and Solar+ Leaders at EU PVSEC 2026.
Research and industry participants used a fictional but recognisable case to explore how leadership, psychological safety, bias, integrity and systems thinking affect innovation. Facilitated groups then identified practical outcomes for leadership behaviour, team practices and cross-sector collaboration.
Know your teams and create shared direction
A central conclusion was that leaders must understand the people behind team roles and connect their contributions to a common objective.
“Leaders and managers need to educate themselves and receive training in cultural aspects, understand their teams better and make the effort to really know them,” said Verónica Bermúdez, Independent Advisor at BERBETIN.
“We also discussed the importance of establishing what common success means and translating that success to the individual teams,” Bermúdez added. “Ultimately, it is a bottom-up approach: the success of the different teams contributes to the overall success of the consortium. But if this is not cascaded from the top, the bottom-up contribution will not work.”
Communication therefore needs to do more than circulate information. It must create transparency and connect individual responsibilities with collective purpose.
“The overarching topic of our discussions was communication: making sure everyone understands not only the success we want to achieve, but also the information needed to get everyone on the same page,” said Walburga Hemetsberger, CEO of SolarPower Europe. “It means being transparent with your teams and making open communication a priority. Communication is the key to success.”
Shared direction does not require uniform thinking. It gives different perspectives enough context to challenge, complement and improve one another.
Create genuine, not performative, participation
Seniority, confidence and communication style can affect which ideas receive attention, regardless of their value. The groups therefore emphasised balancing ego and intentionally creating time for contribution.
“The first thing we realised was how important it is to learn to manage and balance the ego,” said Sarah Albert, Director of Sustainability at Nextpower. “The second is to train ourselves to give everyone the time to speak and be heard.”
“We can practise it in every interaction: with our families, with our friends and then within the business,” she added. “In the meetings we hold, everyone should have the time to speak and be heard.”
Yet inclusion should not become performative. Visible participation does not guarantee trust or influence.
“We discussed trust and the importance of having a clear, common understanding,” said David Moser, Managing Director of Becquerel Institute Italia. “During meetings, it should be safe to speak, but you should not have to. I think that is also important.”
“Even with the best ideas and intentions, when trying to introduce change, you can sometimes become less effective,” Moser explained. “If you are in a meeting and force everyone to speak, it does not necessarily mean it will be a good idea. What matters is that everyone in the room knows that, if they want to say something, they will be heard.”
Psychological safety means having credible ways to contribute without compulsion: during a meeting, in writing, through an agreed process or after time for reflection. What matters is confidence that the contribution will be fairly considered.
Combine leadership responsibility with individual agency
The workshop also challenged the idea that inclusion depends entirely on formal leaders. One group focused on junior professionals whose specialist knowledge may struggle to influence decisions.
“The most striking part of our discussion was how the contribution of people in junior positions, who are well educated and know what they are doing, can be heard,” said Rutger Schlatmann, Head of the Solar Division at Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin.
“It is not only about what leadership should change,” Schlatmann continued. “It is also about how junior team members can come prepared, be assertive and speak up. All members have a responsibility to make sure they are able to contribute.”
Leaders must create environments where those contributions are welcomed, while inclusive cultures should help professionals build the confidence and preparation to exercise their agency. This does not shift responsibility onto less-powerful team members; it connects supportive leadership with individual capability.
Design the conditions for collective intelligence
Across the conclusions, inclusion emerged as part of how innovation is created, not as an objective beside it.
“Inclusion is not something we add to innovation after the priorities have been established and the important decisions have already been made,” said Carmen Madrid, Founder of Women in Solar+ Europe and Solar+ Leaders. “It must be designed into how teams meet, how knowledge is shared, how assumptions are challenged and how different forms of expertise influence decisions from the beginning.”
“When people feel able to contribute their knowledge, question assumptions and share uncertainty, teams can identify risks earlier, develop stronger ideas and make better-informed decisions,” Madrid added. “That is why inclusion is not an initiative sitting alongside innovation. It is how stronger and more responsible innovation becomes possible.”
For PV research–industry partnerships, this means deliberately designing how knowledge is shared, uncertainty communicated, competing interests managed and accountability established. Inclusion is not only about who is represented, but whether their expertise can genuinely shape what happens next.
“Creating space for these conversations is essential because the future of PV depends not only on the technologies we develop, but on how we bring people and expertise together,” said Buse Yıldız, Project Manager at WIP Renewable Energies. “We were delighted to co-organise and host this workshop as part of EU PVSEC and to support an important conversation that can strengthen inclusion, innovation and collaboration across our sector.”

title: Dry August pushes Dallas soiling losses towards 2% as North American GHI diverges - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In a new weekly update for
pv magazine
, Solcast, a DNV company, reports that August irradiance fell across the Great Lakes but rose across the Pacific Northwest, south-central United States, and Mexico amid contrasting weather patterns.
Dry conditions pushed Dallas soiling losses toward a record 2%, while Hurricane Lala brought extreme rain to Hawaii but left monthly irradiance only 4% below normal.
18 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
August produced a sharp divide in irradiance conditions across North America, according to analysis using the
Solcast API
. Global horizontal irradiance (GHI) fell across the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes but rose across the north-west coast and south-central United States and Mexico. Near Dallas, the lack of rain allowed modeled soiling loss to climb towards 2% by the end of the month. Hurricane Lala brought extreme rain to Hawaii, although monthly GHI there was only 4% below normal.
Across much of the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes, GHI was as much as 1715% below average. Chicago recorded a 17% negative anomaly, while Toronto was 10% below average and Buffalo was 8% below. Indiana and Ohio both had their wettest August on record. By contrast, GHI was around 10% above average across the south-central United States as Texas and Oklahoma recorded one of their five driest Augusts. Positive anomalies
continued through most of Mexico. Much of the Pacific Northwest was around 5% above average, while southern California and the interior West were around 5% below.
The anomaly map above shows the contrast between the Great Lakes and the south-central United States and Mexico. These anomalies describe departures from each location’s normal August conditions, rather than absolute irradiance. Below shows the distribution of average daily irradiance, highlighting that despite relative underperformance this year, California remains one of the best places in the country for solar resource.
The continental pattern was associated with a persistent, unusually strong high-pressure ridge centred near the Four Corners and a low-pressure anomaly over Ontario. High pressure suppressed cloud formation across the south-central United States, while the Ontario low supported wetter conditions farther north. Most of the United States also recorded a top-10 or record-warm August. Fires continued in the northwestern United States and British Columbia. Analysis with the Solcast API shows that smoke reduced August GHI by 1–2% across the Northwest and downwind into the north-central United States.
Near Dallas, modeled soiling loss rose towards 2% by the end of August, the highest late-August value in the 2007–2026 series. The increase primarily reflected the absence of rainfall to wash accumulated material from modules, rather than unusually high deposition rates. June soiling was slightly below average and July was above average. August then reached a record high. Across the full June-to-August period, 2026 ranked as the second-highest soiling season on record.
Frequent rains in June kept 2026 soiling close to zero early in summer, then a long dry period allows soiling losses for unwashed panels to rise continuously from mid-July through the end of August.
Hurricane Lala made Hawaii’s first direct hurricane landfall since 1992. Wind gusts reached 90 mph, while flooding brought more than 30 inches of rain, damaged roads and houses, and caused widespread power outages. Hawaii received more than 200% of its average August precipitation, but as the storm only impacted a few days, monthly GHI averaged only 4% below normal. The islands also recorded their third-warmest August in 37 years. Cyclone activity was well above average in the eastern and central Pacific during August but below average in the Atlantic. This distribution was consistent with the strengthening El Niño pattern, which provided warmer Pacific waters to support hurricanes while typically suppressing Atlantic activity.
produces these figures by tracking clouds and aerosols at 1-2km resolution globally, using satellite data and proprietary
AI/ML algorithms
. This data is used to drive irradiance models, enabling Solcast to calculate irradiance at high resolution, with typical bias of less than 2%, and also cloud-tracking forecasts. This data is used by more than 350 companies managing over 350 GW of solar assets globally.

title: Chinese PV Industry Brief: CEEC launches 15 GW module procurement - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
China Energy Engineering Corp. has launched a 15 GW module tender spanning TOPCon, HJT and BC technologies, while China South-to-North Water Diversion Group shortlisted bidders for 1.3 GW, with BC modules commanding an 8% premium over TOPCon.
Vincent Shaw
18 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Inverters
China Energy Engineering Corp
has launched a 15 GW solar module procurement program for 2026, in one of the largest centralized tenders announced by a Chinese state-owned enterprise this year. The procurement covers self-invested and engineering, procurement and construction projects, with separate lots for tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon), heterojunction (HJT), and back-contact (BC) modules. TOPCon is expected to account for the largest share, but the dedicated HJT and BC lots will give both technologies access to a major utility-scale procurement platform. The tender could provide an important gauge of the demand that HJT and BC can capture from TOPCon in large projects, particularly when the final awarded capacities and prices are disclosed.
China South-to-North Water Diversion Group
has named the preferred bidders in a 1.3 GW module framework procurement covering 1 GW of TOPCon products and 300 MW of BC modules. The six shortlisted TOPCon suppliers submitted average bids of approximately CNY 0.72 ($0.10)/W, while the three selected BC suppliers averaged about CNY 0.778/W. The figures imply a BC premium of roughly CNY 0.058/W, or just over 8%. The tender requires minimum module efficiencies of 22.8% for TOPCon products and 23.8% for BC modules. The results provide a relatively rare like-for-like price comparison under a single procurement framework and show that BC technology has progressed beyond pilot projects to several-hundred-megawatt procurement by a major state-owned buyer.
said it is continuing work on its proposed acquisition of 100% of Qinghai Lihao Clean Energy through a combination of share issuance and cash. The company said preliminary auditing and valuation work has been completed, while the parties continue to negotiate the final transaction structure. China’s State Administration for Market Regulation has issued a decision clearing the transaction following an antitrust review. If completed, the acquisition would further strengthen Tongwei’s position in the polysilicon sector. Against a backdrop of persistent oversupply and low utilization rates, the deal is also being closely watched as a potential example of market-driven capacity consolidation.
Golden Solar New Energy Technology
has revised its 2026 private-placement plan, proposing to raise up to CNY 2.39 billion. It plans to allocate CNY 1.69 billion to the first phase of an artificial intelligence computing center in Beijing’s Tongzhou district and CNY 700 million to working capital and debt repayment. The company removed a previously planned Shanghai office and research and development center from the fundraising program. Golden Solar, whose core business remains HJT cells and modules, reported first-half revenue of about CNY 91 million, down 35.2% year on year, and a net loss of approximately CNY 111 million. The revised spending plan highlights how some financially strained solar manufacturers are seeking growth opportunities outside the PV sector.
Jinko Power Technology
is proceeding with an asset-backed securitization program involving 57 commercial and industrial distributed PV plants owned by 34 project companies, with a combined capacity of approximately 298 MW. The holding-type real estate asset-backed special plan is expected to run until 2050, with Jinko Power or related parties set to subscribe to about 10% to 20% of the initial units. The transaction would allow the company to recycle capital tied up in operating solar assets and potentially reinvest the proceeds in new renewable energy projects. The structure also reflects a broader shift among Chinese solar developers toward faster asset turnover and more capital-light development models as project economics and financing conditions become more challenging.

title: Very low cost rooftop solar slashes domestic energy cost - Part 3: African Countries - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
There are 54 countries in the African Continent. Rooftop solar photovoltaics is growing rapidly in some African nations, but uptake is highly uneven across countries and is not measured comprehensively across all nations. It is clear that South Africa is far ahead of the rest of the continent (71% of all rooftop PV in Africa), while Nigeria, Kenya, Morocco and Egypt are emerging as important markets. Despite Africa’s abundant solar resources, a large gap persists between current rooftop solar deployment and its potential, largely due to low residential electricity tariffs and limited access to affordable financing.
International Solar Energy Society (ISES)
18 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Residential
What does the uptake of rooftop solar PV look like in Africa?
Africa has the highest average annual global horizontal irradiation (GHI) of any continent, yet it has the lowest uptake of rooftop solar PV.
Solar PV has been the lowest-cost electricity generation technology for nearly a decade
, and this has resulted in the
fast uptake of this benign technology worldwide
continent-wide rooftop mapping study
estimated that existing rooftop solar installations in Africa represent less than 1% of the continent’s potential, with rooftop PV deployment being primarily driven by local electricity demand, and solar irradiance playing a relatively limited role. South Africa, Nigeria, Morocco, Egypt and Kenya, are the top five rooftop PV adopters in Africa, with roughly 85% of the total. The continent’s technically exploitable rooftop photovoltaics potential area is estimated at nearly 6,000 km2, which, based on average performance coefficient and solar irradiance conversion, can generate more than 2,000 TWh of electricity annually. This theoretical output is more than double Africa’s total electricity generation in 2025.
Residential electricity in Angola is among the cheapest in the world, averaging around $0.015/kWh to $0.030/kWh (approximately AOA 13/kWh to AOA 25/kWh). The most common tier for general households, are typically 50% lower. These low electricity costs are sustained by substantial government subsidies, keeping electricity highly affordable for households while reducing the economic attractiveness of rooftop solar.
Independent power producers (IPPs), many operating thermal plants that burn heavy fuel oil, have long served as Kenya’s stopgap for electricity supply. Long-term contracts with IPPs have locked the country into expensive deals, driving up consumer tariffs. Thermal IPPs supply electricity to Kenya at tariffs as high as $0.23/kWh, making them among the most expensive in the world. By contrast, Kenya buys hydropower from Ethiopia at around $0.066/kWh. But why is the uptake of rooftop PV in Kenya so small if the residential tariffs are so high?
The estimated rooftop PV installed capacity in Kenya is less than 300 MW. This amounts to 5 W per person compared with the 1000 W per person in Australia. High electricity tariffs alone don’t necessarily translate into strong rooftop-PV adoption in Kenya. Several factors work against residential rooftop solar.
1. Households facing the highest tariffs often don’t consume enough electricity; Kenya has a strongly tiered residential tariff structure. In FY2024/25, the lifeline category covered consumption up to 30 kWh/month, while ordinary domestic customers were generally in the 30–100 kWh range and above. That is important because a household consuming 50–100 kWh/month may pay a relatively high price per kWh, but its absolute monthly electricity bill is still small. For perspective, a 1 kW solar PV will produce around 1300 kWh per month.
2. Kenya’s new net-metering regime doesn’t give residential PV full retail value for exports. This is probably one of the most important structural reasons. Kenya introduced a net-metering framework in 2024. Systems can be up to 1 MW, but the initial program is capped at 100 MW over five years. For perspective, Australia has half the population of Kenya and deploys nearly 100 MW of rooftop solar every week. Exported electricity receives a credit equivalent to 50% of the exported energy, rather than the homeowner receiving the full retail electricity price.
3. The upfront capital cost is a much bigger obstacle than the tariff suggests. This is the classic emerging-market problem. A household may have a high marginal electricity tariff but still have limited access to the upfront capital investment required. Ethiopia is the only country in Africa with 100% renewable electricity production, which reflects the country’s abundant hydro resources. This underpins both the domestic affordability and the export competitiveness of Ethiopian electricity but severely limits the attractiveness of rooftop solar PV. In June 2025 Ethiopia inaugurated a 100 kW rooftop system with bidirectional smart meters, described by the government-affiliated Ethiopian News Agency as the country’s first such grid-connected rooftop solar initiative.
Ethiopia

This underpins both the domestic affordability and the export competitiveness of Ethiopian electricity but severely limits the attractiveness of rooftop solar PV. country’s first such grid-connected rooftop solar initiative
Why is rooftop PV adoption so high in South Africa compared with other African countries?
South Africa has an unusually strong combination of a wealthy, grid-connected customer base, unreliable grid electricity, relatively high electricity prices, a high solar radiation resource availability, and a mature solar installation/finance industry. In many other African countries, the economics and customer base are different. Rooftop PV takes off when customers have both the ability to pay for a system and a strong economic reason to minimise grid electricity, on top of high solar radiation resource availability. South Africa has unusually high levels of all the above, and a large “reliability premium”: load shedding. For years, South African households and businesses experienced scheduled electricity outages. That is a very different incentive from a country where the grid is reasonably reliable. That also turned solar PV from an environmental investment into an insurance product: people were installing rooftop PV and, increasingly, batteries because they wanted electricity when Eskom could not provide it. South Africa’s rooftop PV capacity increased from about 1.2 GW in 2020 to roughly 7.3 GW by late 2025. Interestingly, this also provides a natural experiment: when load shedding largely disappeared in 2024, rooftop solar uptake slowed substantially.
The bottom line on rooftop PV adoption
Residential electricity tariffs are a key driver of rapid rooftop PV uptake, while financing conditions, regulatory frameworks, solar irradiation, and declining PV technology costs collectively shape both the pathways and pace of solar adoption across countries. Driven by Chinese panel exports, African nations are on track to install a record
17 GW of total solar in 2026
, with nearly three-quarters of that growth coming from decentralized, distributed systems.

title: Chernobyl ships first processed nuclear waste packages to burial site
content: A major cleanup effort at the Chernobyl disaster site has reached a critical stage. Engineers have completed the first permanent transfer of legacy solid radioactive waste into a dedicated near-surface burial site. Seven sealed packages containing low- and intermediate-level radioactive waste were transported directly to the specialized storage facility known as ENSDF. The repository forms a core section of the Vector complex, located about 130 kilometers north of Kyiv and 20 kilometers south of the Belarusian border.This shipment represents the maiden delivery from the newly commissioned Industrial Complex for Solid Radioactive Waste Management (ICSRM). The complex received official clearance to begin operations late last May, following the approval of an operating license by the State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate of Ukraine. Built with significant financial backing from the European Commission, the site consolidates four distinct technical installations into a single industrial processing line.Managing legacy waste with technical processingDecades after the 1986 disaster, the plant faces a substantial environmental footprint. Large volumes of hazardous material remain stored inside an aging containment repository that has functioned on-site since 1978. Crews must now systematically empty this facility. The stored matter includes everyday industrial refuse accumulated across decades of nuclear power generation. Among the items are discarded personal protective equipment, thermal insulation, electrical cabling, structural steel, rebar, loose soil, building concrete, and exhausted ion-exchange resins taken from water filtration networks.Retrieving these hazardous items requires specialized remote machinery. Technicians extract the material using a dedicated retrieval unit designed to handle roughly 3 cubic meters of solid matter every day. Built for an estimated operational life of three decades, the unit can handle all classes of solid waste found inside the 1978 repository.Once brought to the surface, the retrieved matter is placed inside heavy-duty metal transport containers measuring 1.3 cubic meters. These containers move through an enclosed technological gallery into a fortified hot chamber. The hot chamber serves as the sorting hub. “At this stage, each batch of waste undergoes radiological characterization and control,” said Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in a press release. Any high-level materials unsuited for standard handling are immediately separated.Compaction and decommissioningThe remaining low- and intermediate-level waste is then loaded into 165-liter steel drums. Powerful industrial presses compress the drums to dramatically reduce their volume and stabilize the contents. Once immobilized, these reinforced packages make their final journey across the exclusion zone to the engineered near-surface vaults of the Vector facility.The long-term objective of the ICSRM goes beyond clearing the 1978 storage site. The complex is engineered to handle waste generated by the ongoing decommissioning of Chernobyl’s surviving reactors, alongside operational waste produced during maintenance around the Shelter structure that encloses the ruined fourth reactor.Day-to-day oversight of this hazardous logistics network rests with the Central Enterprise for Radioactive Waste Management, operating under the state-run enterprise SSE CERWM.

title: Electrons seen melting from solid to liquid inside 2D semiconductor
content: Scientists in the US have developed a new approach that allowed them to directly observe how electrons move from a solid-like state into liquid-like waves inside a 2D ultrathin semiconductor.The study was carried out by the US Department of Energy’s Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (Berkeley Lab). For the project, the team used a scanning tunneling microscope and imaged electrons and defects inside a semiconductor made from molybdenum diselenide (MoSe2).The researchers discovered that the number of defects could significantly change electron behavior. The finding could reportedly offer new insights for increasingly miniaturized electronic devices.Mike Crommie, PhD, a Berkeley Lab scientist and UC Berkeley physics professor, said the study offered insights into electron behavior in 2D semiconductors. “Our methods open the door to the discovery of never-seen-before electron behaviors that can be used for new semiconductor capabilities,” he added.Electrons switch statesConventional semiconductor devices, like transistors, computer chips and sensors, are usually made from silicon-based materials. Inside, silicon atoms bond together in a rigid, 3D diamond cubic lattice. This allows billions of transistors to be packed onto a single chip.However, in recent years scientists have increasingly explored 2D semiconductors, ultra-thin materials made from just one or a few layers of atoms. Their super-thin structure changes how electrons behave, potentially enabling new capabilities in future semiconductor devices.Experimental and simulated images show electrons transitioning from a Wigner solid to a Fermi liquid. Credit: Berkeley LabThe team now focused on electrons in a state known as a Wigner solid, an exotic state of matter in which free electrons freeze into a rigid, crystal-like grid instead of flowing like a fluid. In conventional semiconductor devices, electrons behave more like independent particles moving through a material. This state is known as a Fermi liquid.In a Wigner solid, however, repulsion between electrons becomes dominant. The electrons separate, become largely immobile, and also organize themselves into relatively orderly patterns. Scientists have previously struggled to directly observe how defects affect these strongly interacting electrons. Now, the researchers created a specialized device that placed MoSe2 between a graphite layer and layers of silicon and boron nitride. Tiny holes in the graphite allowed the microscope’s metal tip to scan the semiconductor underneath. They then studied samples with different defect levels and adjusted electron density to track the shift between Wigner solid and Fermi liquid states.Defects alter electron behaviorThe images revealed massive differences depending on the number of defects present. When many defects were present, the electrons became locked into an unexpectedly stable Wigner solid with irregular and disordered patterns.With fewer defects, the electrons instead formed more orderly triangular, crystal-like patterns. These transitioned more readily into the Fermi liquid state. Crommie described his first reaction to seeing the unexpected images. “It was exciting to see the Wigner solid melt into liquid-like waves splashing up against defects,” he elaborated. “We could see how electrons respond to defects in very different ways.”He explained that certain defects acted like large potholes while others acted like tiny speed bumps. The team also needed to confirm that the unusual structures were genuine electron behavior rather than artifacts created by the microscope.For this, they used Quantum Monte Carlo simulations to calculate how strongly interacting electrons should respond to random defects according to quantum mechanics. The simulations closely matched the microscope images.Crommie believes that controlling the location and type of defects could become increasingly important as electronic components shrink. “It also helped us better understand the physics underlying the behaviors we observed in our images,” he concluded in a press release.The study has been published in the journal Nature.
